analysis.one_liner: Ends Medicare's competitive bidding program for home medical equipment suppliers.
analysis.headline: A bill to repeal Medicare's competitive bidding for home medical equipment attracted 259 bipartisan cosponsors but never received a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the Medicare program that awards contracts to the lowest-bidding suppliers of wheelchairs, oxygen tanks, and other home medical equipment, and terminate the contracts already awarded. Suppliers would be paid under the old fee schedule, with the cost offset by giving suppliers of most items slightly smaller inflation-linked payment updates through 2015. The bill attracted 259 cosponsors from both parties but never moved past its first subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Home medical equipment suppliers, who would keep the older, generally higher fee-schedule payment rates instead of the lower prices Medicare obtains through supplier competition, and who would receive damages for terminated contracts paid from the Medicare trust fund. Some beneficiaries who worry about supplier choice under competitive bidding, particularly people who rely on customized complex rehabilitative wheelchairs, would also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals section 1847 of the Social Security Act, the section that created the competitive acquisition program in which Medicare awards contracts to the lowest-bidding suppliers of durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies.

Any contracts already awarded under the bidding program would be terminated, and any damages owed because of the terminations would be paid from the Medicare Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund, with no right to challenge the termination in court.

To offset the cost, the bill gives suppliers of complex rehabilitative power wheelchairs inflation-level payment updates (plus 2 points in 2014) and gives suppliers of most other items payment updates set below inflation, 0.25 to 0.5 percentage points lower, through 2015.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries, who would pay 20% copays based on higher fee-schedule prices rather than lower competitively bid prices, and taxpayers, who fund Medicare and would forgo the savings the bidding program was designed to produce. Suppliers of most equipment would also take slightly smaller payment updates to fund the repeal.

drawbacks.text: Competitive bidding exists to lower the amounts Medicare pays suppliers when they compete for contracts; repealing it ends that mechanism and keeps equipment prices at the older fee-schedule levels.
Terminating already-awarded contracts would obligate the Medicare trust fund to pay damages to suppliers, and the bill strips any right to administrative or judicial review of those terminations.

The bill's budget-neutral offset trims annual payment updates for most equipment below inflation from 2010 through 2015, meaning the repeal is funded by squeezing payments to much of the same supplier community it helps.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main beneficiaries are suppliers, who would keep payment rates above what competition would produce, while beneficiaries pay higher copays and taxpayers forgo the bidding program's savings. The genuine concern on the other side — that bidding could disrupt access to customized complex rehabilitative wheelchairs for disabled users — is real but narrow, and the bill addresses it by rolling back the entire program rather than carving out those products. On balance, the cost of the repeal to Medicare and its beneficiaries outweighs the narrower access benefit.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with 16 original cosponsors, the bill was sent to two House committees and then a health subcommittee, where it sat with no markup and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Kendrick Meek of Florida introduced the bill on October 13, 2009, joined by 16 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.
On October 14, 2009, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
The bill accumulated 259 cosponsors, 155 of 253 House Democrats and 104 of 178 House Republicans.
No committee or floor action followed the subcommittee referral, and the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The suppliers who pushed the repeal did not get it. Because the repeal was never enacted, the competitive bidding program created by section 1847 stayed on the books, so Medicare and its beneficiaries retained the lower bid-based payment structure the bill would have removed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medicare and beneficiaries, who kept competitive bidding

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan, with 155 of 253 House Democrats and 104 of 178 House Republicans signing on; there was no recorded opposition because the bill never received a committee markup or floor vote.

industries.note: Repealing competitive bidding would lock in the older fee-schedule payment rates instead of the lower prices Medicare obtains when suppliers compete for contracts, and suppliers would be paid damages for terminated contracts out of the Medicare trust fund. Their gain comes directly out of what Medicare and its beneficiaries pay for the same equipment.

The bill guarantees these suppliers full CPI-level payment updates, plus 2 extra points in 2014, for group 3 and higher power wheelchairs. This tracks a real beneficiary concern that bidding could disrupt access to highly customized wheelchairs for disabled Medicare users.
